content:
At a hearing held today, Apple is challenging the UK government's refusal to publicly confirm whether it has issued a request demanding access to users' encrypted data. Here are the details.

A bit of background

Earlier last year, The Washington Post reported that the UK government had secretly ordered Apple to build a security backdoor into all content uploaded by global users to iCloud.

The order itself is also subject to strict secrecy rules, and even Apple is not permitted to publicly confirm or discuss the request.

The UK government has long maintained a policy of "neither confirm nor deny" the existence of such individual orders, and companies that receive them are likewise prohibited from disclosing that they have done so.

In response to the reported but unconfirmed order, Apple has removed the option to enable Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for iCloud users in the UK.

The reason is that once ADP is enabled, iCloud backups and other categories of iCloud data are protected by end-to-end encryption. As a result, rather than complying with the UK's backdoor order, Apple simply stopped offering ADP to new users in the UK, even though the reported order applied to users worldwide.

At this point, Apple's standoff with the UK government has split into two fronts: challenging the underlying demand for access to encrypted data, and opposing the gag order that prevents it from publicly discussing that demand.

In April 2025, a judge rejected the UK government's attempt to keep even the basic details of Apple's legal challenge secret, ruling that disclosing the existence of the case would not harm national security.

Months later, under pressure from the White House, the UK government dropped its demand for access to US users' data within the scope of the secret authorisation. However, the demand did not disappear entirely: the UK subsequently issued a new notice specifically targeting Apple users within the UK.

Fast forward to a few weeks ago, when reports emerged that Apple had launched a second legal challenge against the UK government after the original global order was replaced by a new order specifically targeting UK users.

Which brings us to today's developments.

Apple challenges the secrecy surrounding the order

According to Reuters, Apple challenged the UK government's continued refusal to confirm or deny the existence of a new "Technical Capability Notice" at a hearing held today at London's Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT).

According to Reuters, Apple's representative counsel argued that the government's secrecy policy hinders meaningful public discussion of the case and undermines the principle of open justice.

Excerpts from the report are as follows:

At Thursday's hearing at the IPT, Ben Jaffey, the lawyer representing the advocacy groups Privacy International and Liberty, said the government's position had become "absurd." He noted that "the horse has bolted," meaning the information was already public. He pointed out that US politicians and officials had publicly mentioned the original notice, and unnamed UK government sources had also confirmed the matter to the media. Both he and Apple's lawyers argued that the UK government's "neither confirm nor deny" policy was an insult to open justice and impeded meaningful public discussion of the issues.

To be clear, today's hearing focused on the secrecy arrangements surrounding the order, not the fundamental legal question of whether the UK government had the initial right to demand access to Apple's encrypted data.

After today's hearing concludes, the IPT will decide whether the government can continue to apply its "neither confirm nor deny" policy in this case. According to Reuters, the full hearing on Apple's challenge to the Technical Capability Notice itself is not expected to take place until after next year.
